name: Calculating the Average of Floating-Point Numbers
description: Construct a program that reads a series of non-negative floating-point numbers from the user, sums them up, and calculate their average.\nNote that you need to think what value should the program use to indicate the end of the input.

comments.content: We need variable total to maintain a running total, which means the sum of the numbers that the user enters. Note that we need to define num as double because it should store the sum of floating-point numbers that we receive from the user.
We need variable count to count how many numbers the user enters. This is required for calculating the average of the numbers that the user enters.
We need variable average to store the average of the numbers entered by the user.
We need to read and process the numbers that the user enters. To read the input numbers from the user, we need to define a Scanner object.

We can create a Scanner object using the operator new, as shown in this statement. The System.in object represents the standard input stream, which by default is the keyboard. It tells the java compiler that the input will be provided through keyboard.
We prompt the user to enter a number.
We read the first number that the user enters and store it in a variable. We read the input by calling the nextDouble() method because the input could have a decimal point.
Note that this can only be done if user input could be translated into a valid double value.

We need to process the number that the user has entered and repeat receiving and processing the numbers from the user as long as the user enters a number that is not negative. Therefore, we need to use a loop structure. Since we don't know ahead of time how many times the loop will be repeated, we need to use a while loop. The condition in the while loop tests whether the body of the loop should be repeated, so it should test whether the input number is not a negative number.

We could test whether the input number is non-negative by testing if the number is greater than or equal to zero.

The body of the while loop is repeated as long as the user enters a number that is greater than or equal to zero. The loop terminates when the loop condition evaluates to false, that is when the user enters a negative number.

We have to count the number of values that are entered because we need it for calculating the average. Therefore, each time that the user enters a number, we need to increment the number of values that user has entered by 1. Note that if the user enters 0, it will not be counted.

The increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable count and the result is stored back into the variable count. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement count = count + 1. Note that the two plus signs that make up the operator cannot be separated by white space.
We need to add the number that the user has entered to the running total. So, each time that the user enters a number, that number needs to be added to and stored back into total.

The += operator adds the value on the right-hand side of the assignment operator (i.e., value of variable num) to the current value of the variable on the left-hand side (i.e., value of variable total) and the result is stored in the variable total. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement total = total + num.

Each time the body of the while loop is repeated, the sum and the number of the values that the user has entered will be printed to the default standard output stream. We do this to see how sum and count are updated after each repeat of the loop. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
The expression in the argument of the println method returns a string that is obtained by concatenating the given strings and value of the variables.
We prompt the user to enter the next number.

We need to read the next number that the user enters but this needs to be done only after we have added the previous number to the running total and we updated the count. Therefore, the next number must be read in the end of the loop body. If we read the next number in the beginning of the loop body, then the first number that the user has entered would not be added to the sum or counted which will result in an incorrect calculation of the sum and average.
We read the number by calling the nextDouble() method because the input could have a decimal point.
Note that this can only be done if user input could be translated into a valid double value.
We close the scanner as we do not want to process any input from the user in the rest of the program.

We need the if statement at the end of the program to avoid a divide-by-zero error. This occurs if the user immediately enters a negative number before entering any other number.

To determine if the divide-by-zero error would occur, we need to test if the number of values entered by the user is equal to zero.
If the number of values that the user has entered is equal to zero, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
This statement prints to the default standard output stream that no numbers were entered. This text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

If the above if test fails (i.e., when the number of values the the user has entered is different from zero), we could calculate the average by dividing the sum by the number of values entered by the user.

We need to calculate the average by dividing the sum of the values by the number of the values that the user entered. Notice that one of the variables in the division (variable total) is a double and the other variable (variable count) is an int. In this case, when floating-point value total is divided by an integer value count, the value of count is promoted to a floating-point value automatically, before the division takes place; thus, producing a floating-point result.

We want to round the average to three decimal places. To do this, we need to instantiate a DecimalFormat object with a pattern. In this statement, the pattern defined by the string 0.### indicates that at least one digit should be printed to the left of the decimal point and should be a zero if the integer portion of the value is zero. It also indicates that the fractional portion of the value should be rounded to three digits.

This statement prints the calculated average to the default standard output stream. Note that the average is formatted to have maximum of three decimal places. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
The expression in the argument of the println method returns a string that is obtained by concatenating the given string and value of the formatted variable.
